cards.title: The corrections issue
cards.body: Today's thread is corrections: settled pictures that turn out to be wrong. The one not to miss is the axon — the cable a brain cell sends its signal down. Textbooks have drawn it as a smooth tube for a hundred years, and careful new imaging shows something closer to a string of pearls, which quietly changes the neuron picture you have carried since school. Two more sit beside it: a physicist argues the famous quantum puzzle may have started with a choice Schrödinger himself made, and a new book says nothing is really lost when you squash a clay statue.

cards.title: Textbook axons are smooth. Real ones look like pearls.
cards.body: For a hundred years, students learned the axon — the cable a brain cell sends its signal down — as a smooth, narrow tube. Freeze mouse neurons fast instead of drying them out, and the tube turns out to be a string of tiny pearls. The shape is not decoration. It changes how fast the signal travels, and hard use makes the pearls swell.
cards.evidence: single study · mouse neurons, nonmyelinated axons · high pressure freezing electron microscopy, live imaging, modelling

sections.text:
The drawing has not changed in a hundred years. A blob for the cell body, a spray of short branches, and one long smooth cable running off the edge of the page. That cable is the axon — the wire a brain cell uses to send its electrical signal to the next cell. The textbook gives it a few bulges. Those are synapses, the handover points, full of neurotransmitters — the chemicals one cell passes to another. Between them: a clean, narrow tube.

Now the new picture. A team at Johns Hopkins looked at mouse axons and found small swellings repeating all the way along, like pearls on a string. They are not synapses. The team calls them non-synaptic varicosities — bulges that are not handover points. The work appeared in Nature Neuroscience in December 2024. Shigeki Watanabe, who led it, says it challenges a century of understanding.

The pivot was not a new idea. It was a new way of preparing tissue. An axon is about a hundred times thinner than a human hair, so you need an electron microscope to see one. The usual method treats the tissue with chemicals and dries it out — steps that can quietly change the shape you came to measure. This team froze it under high pressure instead. Watanabe's comparison: freeze a grape rather than dry it into a raisin. Across tens of thousands of images, the same pearls. Live imaging of working neurons showed them too, so the freezing was not inventing them.

Their first guess was that a scaffold inside held the shape. Jacqueline Griswold, the first author, broke that inner skeleton. The pearls stayed. So the team looked outward, to the membrane — the axon's skin — and modelled it with biophysicist Padmini Rangamani. Simple physics gave the same pearls, with no stiff mould needed. Pull the membrane tighter, by adding sugar to the liquid around it, and the pearls shrank. Take out cholesterol, which leaves the membrane floppier, and the pearls changed and the signal slowed. Wide stretches let ions — the charged particles that carry the current — through without a traffic jam. But bigger was not always faster. The narrow necks between the pearls mattered too.

Then the part that makes this more than a drawing. After hard electrical stimulation, the pearls grew: about 8% longer and 17% wider, still swollen half an hour later, with signals slowed for at least an hour. The wire had been reshaped by its own use. A related study has since found pearled axons in human brain tissue taken during epilepsy surgery.

Hold it loosely. This is one group re-describing one structure, not a finished replacement for the textbook.

And still, a smooth tube teaches something it never says out loud: that the axon is plumbing. Fixed. Passive. Interesting only at its ends. A hundred years of students learned where to look for the action, and it was never the middle of the cable.

sections.label: Key takeaways
items: Then: a smooth narrow tube with a few bulges, and every bulge a synapse.
Now: pearls repeating all along it, and most are not synapses at all.
The pivot: high pressure freezing instead of chemicals and drying. Grape, not raisin.
What it buys: shape changes signal speed, and hard use changes the shape.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: Mouse neurons, and bare ones — no myelin, the insulating cover that wraps many axons. The human follow-up looked mainly at how nerve endings recycle membrane. It does not show that every human axon is pearled, or that pearling does the same job everywhere in the brain. Beads along axons are also an old sight in dying neurons and in Parkinson's disease, where they come with damage. Telling healthy pearls from that damage is still open, and the team names it as their next question.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The textbook was not lying. It was drawing a raisin and calling it the grape.

recall.q: The pearls were there all along. What kept them out of the picture for a century?
recall.a: Not a missing idea — a preparation step. The standard method treats tissue with chemicals and dries it, which can change the very shape you are trying to measure. Freezing it fast under high pressure instead — a grape rather than a raisin — kept the pearls intact.

cards.title: The oven can cook the lamb. It cannot taste it.
cards.body: In a Silicon Valley basement in 2015, two chefs cooked a farm's worth of meat to teach a prototype oven their recipes. They tasted every result and filled in forms. The oven could hold a heat no human hand can hold. It could not taste a thing.

sections.text:
The basement was full of smoke. Silicon Valley, summer 2015, under an office building. Wall ovens stood stacked on trolleys. Cords ran behind a steel counter. On a prep table sat a small machine that looked like a microwave built for one cupcake. It was a moisture analyser: it measured how much juice was left in a piece of lamb or swordfish.

The company wanted an oven that made restaurant food at the press of one button. Two chefs were hired to cook a farm's worth of meat into it. They tasted every result and filled in forms: colour, smell, temperature, texture, taste. The smoke had a cause. One chef had pushed three racks of lamb straight under the broiler, the oven's fierce top heat, chasing the colour you get from "smacking it" with a blowtorch. The oven had no setting for smacking.

Liam Spradlin was there as design lead for the oven's touchscreen. His job pulled two ways. The chefs wanted controls they could adjust by hand. The company wanted the home cook to have almost none. Changing a recipe would fight the oven's smarts and risk a bad dinner. "Change the ritual" was written on the whiteboards.

The oven could read moisture to a decimal point and hold a heat no human hand can hold. It could not taste. Not ever. The forms the chefs filled in were not the oven learning taste. They were taste turned into numbers, so the machine could work without it.

Spradlin has an image for it: you cannot taste a cherry by counting the petals on the tree. Count as long as you like. The blossom is real. It is not the fruit. Asking a machine to judge taste, the designer Nitzan Hermon says, is like asking a stone which films it likes. Not a hard question. The wrong kind of question.

He has a name for the belief under the oven: computism. The idea that the world, people included, is made of parts you can measure — so everything can be computed, predicted, improved. Believe that, and the person in the middle stops looking like the point and starts looking like the fault.

Which brings you to tonight. A paid service called Wonder now assigns its users three meals a day. It reads their fitness goals, likes and hunger, then decides what they will eat. Spell-checkers have grown into tools that tell you how to sound, built from other people's writing. In June 2026 a startup announced that taste itself is a data problem: with enough extra training, a model can make great works of taste.

Each time, on its own, the machine's version is the sensible choice. It is faster. It is usually better. Deciding is tiring. The chef holding three racks of lamb under the broiler was not being efficient. He was doing the exact thing the oven was built to remove.

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: The company's fear was not silly. A home cook who changes a recipe really can ruin dinner. An oven that holds an exact temperature beats most people's guesswork most nights. Spradlin says he took the vision seriously at the time. The cost is not one spoiled meal. It is that the judging now happens somewhere else, by something that has never eaten.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Count every petal on the tree, and you still have not tasted one cherry.

recall.q: The chefs rated colour, smell, texture and taste for every dish they cooked. Why does the writer say this was not the oven learning to taste?
recall.a: The forms turned taste into numbers the oven could follow. The oven still had no experience of taste at all. Data about a thing can stand in for the thing, so the machine can work without it — like counting blossoms instead of eating the cherry.

cards.title: Day 2 · The 'I' that grammar invented
cards.body: Yesterday Nietzsche put philosophers on the couch. Today he goes after the one thing everyone thought was safe — the "I" in "I think" — and finds grammar where a soul was supposed to be.

sections.text:
Descartes said "I think, therefore I am," and treated it as bedrock. Nietzsche picks the sentence apart.

Say "I think." Count what you just assumed. That it is I who think. That thinking must have a thinker. That thinking is an activity, and every activity needs a doer. That there is an "ego" at all. And last: that you already know what thinking is — otherwise how could you tell this event is thinking and not "willing" or "feeling"? To name your state you must compare it with other states you remember. So the most certain sentence in philosophy quietly leans on memory. It is not immediate at all. His reply to the man who is sure: "it is improbable that you are not mistaken, but why should it be the truth?"

Then the cleanest line of the day: "a thought comes when 'it' wishes, and not when 'I' wish." Sit still and watch your own head. Thoughts arrive. You do not make them. So where does the "I" come from? From grammar. A sentence needs a subject, so we invent one behind the verb. He compares it to old physics: there was a force, so people assumed a little particle for the force to live in — the atom. Physics learned to drop the particle. Maybe one day logic drops the "I".

Next he opens up the will, which Schopenhauer called the one thing we know completely. Nietzsche finds it crowded. In a single act of will there are sensations — the state you move away from, the state you move toward, the "from" and "towards" itself, and a muscle feeling that begins before you move a limb. There is a ruling thought. And above all there is an emotion: the emotion of command.

That is the trick at the center of today. When you will something, you are both the one giving the order and the one obeying it. We hide that split under the little word "I". So when the order gets carried out, the commander takes the credit and feels a rush of power — and that rush is what we call "freedom of the will." L'effet c'est moi: the effect, that's me. The body, he says, is "a social structure composed of many souls," and the ruling class always claims the wins of the whole country.

He widens it. Philosophers feel original, yet they keep circling one orbit, because the grammar of their language decides which thoughts are even available; Indian, Greek and German philosophy look like relatives for that reason. Thinking is less a discovery than "a return and a home-coming."

Then he refuses both sides of the free-will fight. To be causa sui — your own cause — you would have to pull yourself into existence by your own hair, Munchausen-style. But "non-free will" is mythology too. Cause, effect, necessity, law: useful fictions for talking to each other, not explanations. In real life there are only strong wills and weak ones. And watch which side a man takes: some cannot give up their responsibility, out of vanity; others want to be blamed for nothing, out of self-contempt.

The physicists get the same treatment. "Nature's conformity to law" is not a text, it is a reading — and a flattering one, equality before the law, very modern. Someone else could read the same facts as pure Will to Power. Then the honest shrug: "Granted that this also is only interpretation... well, so much the better."

The chapter ends on a dare. Psychology has run aground on moral fear. Suppose hatred, envy, greed and the love of ruling are conditions of life itself, and the good impulses grow out of the bad ones. That thought gives an honest conscience seasickness. Set your teeth, he says, hand on the helm, and sail "right OVER morality."

Chapter II, The Free Spirit, opens strangely gentle. We live in a simplified, falsified world, and that is exactly how we manage to enjoy it; knowledge stands on a "granite-like foundation of ignorance". His advice to thinkers is not courage but care. Beware of martyrdom — suffering for truth makes you stubborn and theatrical, and truth is not so weak that it needs bodyguards. Better to have masks, a garden, good solitude. "And no one is such a LIAR as the indignant man."

sections.label: From the book
sections.text: With regard to the superstitions of logicians, I shall never tire of emphasizing a small, terse fact, which is unwillingly recognized by these credulous minds--namely, that a thought comes when "it" wishes, and not when "I" wish; so that it is a PERVERSION of the facts of the case to say that the subject "I" is the condition of the predicate "think." ONE thinks; but that this "one" is precisely the famous old "ego," is, to put it mildly, only a supposition, an assertion, and assuredly not an "immediate certainty."

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: A thought comes when it wishes. The "I" arrives afterwards, to take the credit.

recall.q: Nietzsche says a thought comes when "it" wishes, not when "I" wish. So where does the "I" in "I think" come from?
recall.a: From grammar. A sentence needs a subject, so we invent a doer behind the activity — the way old physics invented the atom to hold the force. The "ego" is a supposition, not an immediate certainty.
